newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Cyprus president condemns violence at British base.
newsitem.headline: Cyprus president condemns violence at British base.

text.p: Cyprus President Glafcos Clerides condemned on Tuesday violent protests at a British base where Greek Cypriots stormed a military police compound and freed two detainees.
"The president of the republic believes that actions of this kind do not promote national interests," government spokesman Manolis Christofides said.

"On the contrary they create problems in the relations of Cyprus with Britain at a crucial phase of the Cyprus problem and (the island's) European course," he said, referring to the current division of the island as well as its application to join the European Union.

Dozens of British soldiers armed with assault rifles were on foot patrol at Episkopi base on Tuesday afternoon after clashes with locals on Monday demanding the release of Greek Cypriot prisoners. Seven people were slightly injured in the violence.

The base has been sealed off, the main road running through it blocked with an armoured personnel carrier and an army truck, its windscreen shattered from a hail of stones which fell on it the night before.
There was no sign of demonstrators, possibly put off by the strong statement by Clerides who "unreservedly condemned" Monday's protests.
Cyprus has been divided since Turkey invaded its north in 1974 in response to a brief coup in Nicosia engineered by the Athens junta.

Britain, a guarantor power, has spurred its own mediation efforts to resolve the dispute. Last year Sir David Hannay, London's former ambassador to the United Nations, was appointed Britain's special representative on the Cyprus problem.

Trouble at Episkopi started when base police detained a Greek Cypriot on charges of building illegally at Trachoni, a village on bases territory close to Episkopi, and assaulting two base officers. Five Cypriots detained in ensuing scuffles have been released and two were still in detention.
Britain has held two military bases in Cyprus since independence in 1960. It enjoys sovereign rights on both, but an increasing number of Greek Cypriots appear to be questioning this arrangement.
Last month a small group of demonstrators pelted stones at a police compound in the Dhekelia base on the southeast, calling for the release of a youth jailed for motoring offences.
"It is the government of Cyprus that represents the people of Cyprus, not this self-appointed minority representing no one but themselves," base administrator Peter Millar said.
